newsitem.title: UK: Dlr seen avoiding gold's fate in EMU reserve rejig.
newsitem.headline: Dlr seen avoiding gold's fate in EMU reserve rejig.

text.p: Growing interest in the rationale behind recent European central bank gold sales has again raised the issue of a potential currency market impact from central bank reserve shifts after European monetary union (EMU).

The gold price, which hit its lowest level in almost four years today, has clearly suffered from recent large-scale Dutch and Belgian central bank sales, the proceeds of which have been used to pay off outstanding public debt.
But, analysts believe that a pan-European political interest in maintaining a strong dollar is likely to prevent a similar fate befalling the continent's massive dollar reserves.

"It looks like Europe is going to go into monetary union with a very formidable war chest of dollar reserves, probably far more than they actually need," said Julian Callow, economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.

"But, the problem is like having a nuclear arsenal with no one who wants to press the button. The finance ministers will not want the ECB to sell its dollars if it ends up weakening the U.S. currency."
The issue of debt reduction from reserve sales was raised earlier this week, however.
The European Union's statistics body Eurostat ruled that the proceeds from central bank gold sales could not be used directly to cut national budget deficits.
But, Belgian officials claimed that Eurostat, on the initiative of the Belgian National Bank, accepted that gold sales can be used to cut outstanding debt.
Analysts say the temptation to sell robust levels of idle dollar reserves and repay chunks of national debt ahead of EMU may be also tempting but several reasons militate against this.
Firstly, the interest earned on currency reserves can be treated as government revenue and used as such to bolster current spending and ease budget deficit burdens.
The loss of this potential interest by cutting dollar reserves, for example, would at least partly negate the savings from a reduction of interest payments on outstanding debt.

More importantly, however, analysts argue that the perceived political influence on the conduct of European central bank policy after EMU, promoted in particular by the French, will ensure a reluctance to weaken the dollar against the new euro.
It is argued that the very existence of huge dollar reserves will prevent any collapse in confidence in the new single currency, because of the their potential mobilisation in any such crisis.
Extensive studies have been conducted by market economists over the past year on the reconfiguration of reserves after EMU.

Opinions vary but the one underlying theme is European central banks will end up holding billions of dollars of reserves after EMU, mostly denominated in the U.S. unit, which are far in excess of estimates of what they need.

A possible eight-country euro area of Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Austria, Ireland and Finland is estimated to have a total of more than $200 billion worth of foreign exchange reserves at present.

The reserves these countries denominated in each other's currencies (mainly German marks) will automatically be converted to euros, or domestic currency, on EMU day. This will lead to the effective disappearance of as much as $50 billion which will no longer be foreign exchange, analysts said.

"If anything, it's likely European central banks have been offloading their mark reserves for dollars in order to prevent this virtual disappearance of fx and as they prepare to hand over a proportion of reserves to the ECB," said Adrian Schmidt, economist at Chase Investment Bank.
Schmidt said this is likely to have been a key factor in the dollar's steady rise in recent months.
Yet, even with that reduction the euro zone will still have $150 billion of reserves, almost entirely in dollars.
There are two ways of judging what sort of "excess" this represents.

For one, the Maastricht Treaty only requires 50 billion European currency units (about $58 billion) to be transferred to the ECB at the start of EMU. That still leaves an excess of about $90 billion in EU coffers.

Another way of looking at optimal levels of ECB reserves assesses the average import-to-reserves ratio in industrial countries at present, where level of reserves typically corresponds with a country's essential import bill for period during any emergency.
On this basis the ECB would only need about $80 billion.

A question that has concerned economists is whether fiscally-strapped European governments will accumulate a potential windfall by selling the "excess" dollars over time and repaying large levels of outstanding debt.
To date, gold has been the whipping boy, partly because European central banks typically hold a greater proportion of it in their reserves than other central banks around the world.
In December, Belgium used 230 billion francs of proceeds from past gold sales to pay off foreign currency borrowings.

The Netherlands confirmed in January it sold 300 tonnes of central bank gold in 1996, raising $3.8 billion which it would hold as interest-bearing foreign currency reserves and in effect adding to its already substantial forex reserves.
The Dutch said the interest earned would form part of the bank's profit transferred to the government as revenue, thereby reducing the Netherlands' deficit.
"I think the authorities are aware that this sort of disturbance to the gold price is not desirable and I'm not sure we will see too much more of this," said Callow at Kleinwort.
It may be that Europe will end up resisting the temptation to pare its bloated debt levels and simply allow its embarrassment of reserve riches after EMU to gather dust.
"These level of dollar reserves are a bit of a waste and, to an extent, an economic cost, but it looks like they may well stay put for some time," said Schmidt at Chase.
